analysis.one_liner: Admits the District of Columbia into the Union as the State of New Columbia, with two senators and a representative.
analysis.headline: The bill, reported out of committee on a 7–4 vote in September 1992, never received a House floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make most of the District of Columbia a state called New Columbia, keeping a small federal enclave for the White House, Capitol, Supreme Court, and monuments. The new state would get two senators and one House member, and its roughly 600,000 residents — who today pay federal taxes but have no voting member of Congress — would gain full representation. Admission would require a vote of District residents to ratify it.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of the District of Columbia, a majority-Black city of about 600,000 people who pay federal taxes but have no voting representation in Congress and whose local laws Congress can override. They would gain two senators, one representative, and full control of their own government.

how_it_helps.text: Admits New Columbia 'on an equal footing with the other States in all respects,' entitling it to two senators and one representative [S2][S3].

Carves out a small National Capital Service Area for federal buildings and monuments, addressing the constitutional concern about a federal seat inside a state, and leaves federal property tax-exempt [S3].
Requires District voters themselves to approve statehood, boundaries, and the terms of admission in a ratification election before the President can proclaim admission [S3].
Continues the annual federal payment to the new state and requires the governor to report on revenues lost because of federal presence, such as tax-exempt property and building-height limits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Existing members of Congress, who would lose direct control over District lawmaking, and the balance of Senate power, which would shift by two seats. Federal taxpayers continue an existing annual payment to the new state, which the bill does not change.

drawbacks.text: Critics of D.C. statehood argue a single city of under a million people should not hold two Senate seats, a point of real constitutional and political debate not resolved by the record here.

The bill entrenches some federal control even as it grants statehood: Congress must consent to any change in the city's building-height rules, and federal military lands stay under exclusive federal jurisdiction [S3].
The bill was introduced by the non-voting Delegate with zero cosponsors, so it never demonstrated broad support even within the House [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people affected, the gain is substantial and the cost small: full voting representation and self-government for a taxed population, at the price of a temporary extra House seat and a continued federal payment. The genuine objection is structural — whether one city deserves two senators — but the bill answers the federal-seat problem directly with its enclave carve-out. The main weakness was not design but support: no cosponsors and no floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: The District of Columbia Committee approved it 7–4 and formally reported it to the House in September 1992, but House leadership never brought it up for a vote before the 102nd Congress expired in January 1993.

narrative.text: Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the New Columbia Admission Act on March 31, 1992, and it was referred to the House Committee on District of Columbia [S1][S5].
On April 2, 1992, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported by a vote of 7 to 4 [S5].
On September 25, 1992, the committee reported the bill (H. Rept. 102-909) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the queue of bills awaiting floor action [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a House floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of D.C. statehood, including members of Congress who preferred keeping the District under federal control, were better off: the bill died without a vote, and District residents remained without voting representation in Congress.

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.role: Delegate (non-voting) representing the District of Columbia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through committee markup and reporting.

for.name: 7 members of the House Committee on the District of Columbia
for.what_they_did: Voted 7–4 to order the bill reported to the full House.

against.name: 4 members of the House Committee on the District of Columbia
against.what_they_did: Voted no when the committee ordered the bill reported.

against.name: House leadership of the 102nd Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it was reported and placed on the Union Calendar.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no cosponsors of either party, and the 7–4 committee vote to report it showed the divided committee; D.C. statehood in this era divided sharply along party lines, with Republicans uniformly opposed and Democrats sympathetic but not enough to bring it to the floor.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress (as holders of power over the District)
industries.note: Congress currently exercises exclusive legislative authority over the District and can override its local laws; statehood would end that control and add two senators, shifting Senate power. The interest in retaining that control runs directly against residents' self-government. [S2][S3]

industries.industry: Federal government (as landowner and employer in the District)
industries.note: The bill keeps federal property tax-exempt, reserves a federal enclave and military lands under exclusive federal jurisdiction, and requires Congress's consent to change building-height rules, but it also obligates the state to study and report on revenues lost to the federal presence. [S3]
